short: The United States has no comprehensive federal AI statute. Federal AI policy runs through executive orders and OMB memoranda, one narrow statute reaches AI forgeries (the TAKE IT DOWN Act), the FTC enforces existing law, and the binding AI laws are the states'.
title: United States AI Laws
subtitle: No federal AI act: executive orders, one narrow statute, the FTC, and the states
body_html:
Status at a glance

No federal AI act; the states and sector law bind. Congress has passed no comprehensive AI statute. Federal AI policy runs through executive orders and Office of Management and Budget memoranda, which bind federal agencies, not companies. One federal statute reaches AI output by name: the TAKE IT DOWN Act, which criminalises publishing non-consensual intimate depictions, including AI "digital forgeries", and requires platforms to remove them. The Federal Trade Commission applies section 5 of the FTC Act to deceptive and unfair AI practices. The binding AI laws in the United States are the states', tracked state by state on AI laws by state. Verified on 25 October 2026 against GovInfo, the White House, the Department of Justice and the FTC.

Key instruments

InstrumentNumberSigned or enactedWhat it does
Initial Rescissions of Harmful Executive Orders and ActionsEO 1414820 January 2025Revoked EO 14110 of 2023 (sec. 2)
Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial IntelligenceEO 14179, 90 FR 874123 January 2025Directs an AI Action Plan and a review of actions taken under the revoked EO 14110
Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public TrustOMB M-25-213 April 2025Replaces M-24-10; Chief AI Officers, agency AI strategies, minimum practices for high-impact AI
TAKE IT DOWN ActPub. L. 119-12, adding 47 U.S.C. 223(h)Approved 19 May 2025Criminalises publishing non-consensual intimate depictions, including digital forgeries; platform notice-and-removal within one year of enactment
Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial IntelligenceEO 14365, 90 FR 5849911 December 2025A DOJ task force to challenge state AI laws (sec. 3); Commerce review of state laws, NTIA funding conditions and an FTC policy statement within 90 days
Artificial Intelligence Litigation Task ForceAttorney General memorandum9 January 2026Sets up the task force EO 14365 ordered
Proposed Policy Statement Concerning the Suppression of Accuracy in AI SystemsFTC, 91 FR 41638Proposed 7 July 2026The FTC's statement under EO 14365, sec. 7; not final

Who regulates and enforces

  • Federal Trade Commission: section 5 of the FTC Act against deceptive and unfair practices, and the TAKE IT DOWN Act's notice-and-removal duty. See FTC AI enforcement.
  • Department of Justice: prosecutes TAKE IT DOWN Act offences; its AI Litigation Task Force challenges state AI laws.
  • Office of Management and Budget: governs federal agencies' own AI use (M-25-21).
  • State attorneys general and agencies: enforce the state AI laws. See State AI Laws and Agency Enforcement.

Scope and reach

The executive orders and M-25-21 bind federal agencies; M-25-21 covers independent regulatory agencies and excludes national security systems. The TAKE IT DOWN Act reaches anyone who publishes a covered depiction, and "covered platforms" must run a notice-and-removal process (sec. 3). State laws set their own reach, often by where consumers or applicants live.

Core obligations

  • Covered platforms: a process to receive and act on removal requests for non-consensual intimate depictions (TAKE IT DOWN Act, sec. 3).
  • Federal agencies: Chief AI Officers, AI strategies and minimum practices for high-impact AI (M-25-21).
  • Everyone else: existing federal law, such as the FTC Act, civil rights and credit statutes (see Sector Rules), and the state AI laws.

Penalties

BreachMaximumProvisionEnforcer
Publishing an intimate depiction or digital forgery of an adult without consentA fine, imprisonment of up to 2 years, or both47 U.S.C. 223(h), added by Pub. L. 119-12DOJ
The same, of a minorA fine, imprisonment of up to 3 years, or both47 U.S.C. 223(h)DOJ
Threats using digital forgeriesUp to 18 months (adult) or 30 months (minor), a fine, or both47 U.S.C. 223(h)DOJ
A covered platform failing the notice-and-removal dutyTreated as a violation of an FTC rulePub. L. 119-12, sec. 3(b)FTC
State AI law violationsSet by each state; see each state's pageAI laws by stateState attorneys general and agencies

What is coming next

  • A final FTC policy statement on AI accuracy, proposed 7 July 2026.
  • Congressional action on the White House's National AI Legislative Framework of 20 March 2026, and on federal preemption bills; none has been enacted.
  • State legislative sessions: every bill is tracked on AI laws by state.
